title: Jeremiah 18:18–23
context: The people plot against Jeremiah, determined to discredit him and ignore his words. Jeremiah turns to the LORD, reminding him that he once interceded for these very people, and then prays that judgment fall on them and their families. This is one of Jeremiah’s prayers often called his confessions, honest cries spoken in prayer rather than doctrine stated for imitation. Both traditions read his words within the setting of persecution and prophetic calling, and both commit vengeance to God rather than to human hands.

verses.text: Then they said, “Come! Let’s devise plans against Jeremiah; for the law won’t perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, and let’s strike him with the tongue, and let’s not give heed to any of his words.”
verses.arminianNotes: Let’s devise plans against Jeremiah; Arminian readers see the people choosing to silence the prophet rather than heed him, confident that priests, sages, and prophets will remain without him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the people’s plan to strike him with the tongue, through slander or accusation. Opposition to God’s word often takes the form of discrediting the messenger.

verses.text: Give heed to me, LORD, and listen to the voice of those who contend with me.
verses.arminianNotes: Give heed to me, LORD, and listen to the voice of those who contend with me. Arminian readers see Jeremiah turning his distress into prayer, bringing his case directly to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Jeremiah answers the plot not by retaliation but by appeal to God. His prayer begins with a plea to be heard, a pattern found in the Psalms.

verses.text: Should evil be recompensed for good? For they have dug a pit for my soul. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them.
verses.arminianNotes: Should evil be recompensed for good? For they have dug a pit for my soul. Arminian readers note that Jeremiah had interceded for these people, and their hostility felt like betrayal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the prophet’s reminder, Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them. His prayer arises from wounded love as much as from anger.

verses.text: Therefore deliver up their children to the famine, and give them over to the power of the sword. Let their wives become childless and widows. Let their men be killed and their young men struck by the sword in battle.
verses.arminianNotes: Therefore deliver up their children to the famine, and give them over to the power of the sword. Arminian readers acknowledge that the prayer is shocking and do not soften it, while reading it as an appeal for God’s justice, compared with the imprecatory language of Psalm 109:6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read it as committing vengeance to God rather than taking it into human hands. Christians read such prayers in light of Christ’s command to love enemies (see the Matthew 5:44 box), without explaining away the prophet’s anguish.

verses.text: Let a cry be heard from their houses when you bring a troop suddenly on them; for they have dug a pit to take me and hidden snares for my feet.
verses.arminianNotes: Let a cry be heard from their houses when you bring a troop suddenly on them; Arminian readers see Jeremiah asking that the judgment he has announced come to pass on those who reject and hunt him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the plea aligns with what God has already said he will do. The prophet prays for God’s word to be fulfilled, though his words remain raw and painful.

verses.text: Yet, LORD, you know all their counsel against me to kill me. Don’t forgive their iniquity. Don’t blot out their sin from your sight, Let them be overthrown before you. Deal with them in the time of your anger.
verses.arminianNotes: Yet, LORD, you know all their counsel against me to kill me. Don’t forgive their iniquity. Arminian readers hear a cry from a man whose life is threatened, and they read it as honest prayer rather than a pattern for believers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prayer leaves judgment to God’s time, Deal with them in the time of your anger. Both traditions read it pastorally as a cry of the persecuted, preserved so that such anguish may be brought to God.
